summary: No department-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for El Callao appears in the sources. The one item anchored in the department is the July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom signage at Jorge Chávez international airport, the country's principal international gateway, which sits in El Callao; that complaint is reported as the trigger for the congressional measure restricting public sanitary facilities to birth sex. Everything else a trans visitor encounters in El Callao is delivered by national law and national enforcement, and the national assessment applies.
tangentialFactors: The restroom-signage complaint that prompted the national measure concerned the airport in El Callao. The enforcement mechanism described by activist Gianna Camacho, security staff checking the national identity document to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, would therefore be met first by arriving visitors at that airport, before they reach any other part of the country.
localsOnly: A 2012 study by Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao worked in sex work, a documented exposure factor for police and public violence. No Callao-specific enforcement action, prosecution or protection measure appears in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes: No source in the inventory reports an El Callao ordinance, municipal measure, prosecution or police action bearing on trans residents or visitors. Whether the national restroom restriction has been enforced at Jorge Chávez airport or elsewhere in the department is not documented. Peru's crime-registration systems do not record sexual orientation or gender identity, so no Callao-specific hate-crime count can be isolated from the national figures.
